title: 道德經 第六十八章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 68, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 86. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 68 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 配天 (Matching Heaven). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to be good at, to do well at
the knight-officer; Wang Bi glosses it 卒之帥, 'the commander of the troops' — the man who leads soldiers, not the man in the ranks
the one who — turns everything before it into a noun
martial — here used as a verb: to play the warrior, to make a show of force

sentences.l: The one good at acting as an officer is not warlike;
sentences.i: The best commander of men makes no display of force;
sentences.n:
Four sense-units, four clauses cut to one pattern: 善 'good at' + a verb + 者 'the one who', each answered by a flat 不. 善為士者, 善戰者, 善勝敵者, 善用人者 — the shape is the argument.

士 is the knight-officer, a man of the fighting class with a calling — and Wang Bi is more exact than the dictionaries here: 士，卒之帥也, 'the 士 is the commander of the troops'. The English follows him, so this is the man who leads soldiers, not the man in the ranks. 武 is 'martial' doing duty as a verb, to play the warrior.

Listen to the four line-ends as they come: 武 wǔ, 怒 nù, 與 yǔ, 下 xià. All four belonged to one Old Chinese rhyme group (魚), and three of them still chime in Mandarin; only 下 has drifted out. This is about as close as a modern reader gets to hearing the verse.

morph.gloss: to be good at, to do well at
the one who — turns everything before it into a noun
to be angry, to flare up in rage

sentences.l: the one good at battle does not rage;
sentences.i: the best in battle never lets anger take him;

morph.gloss: to be good at, to do well at
to overcome, to get the better of (shèng)
the one who — turns everything before it into a noun
to join with, to have dealings with, to meet in contest (yǔ)

sentences.l: the one good at overcoming an enemy does not join with him;
sentences.i: the best conqueror of enemies never engages them;
sentences.n: 與 again, and the third of its senses: not 'give', not 'with', but 'to join with, to have dealings with'. Wang Bi says it plainly — 不與爭也, 'he does not join battle with them'. The best conqueror never lets it come to a contest at all.

sentences.t:
善用人者為之下，
是謂不爭之德，
是謂用人之力，

morph.gloss: to be good at, to do well at
to use, to put to use
the one who — turns everything before it into a noun
their (genitive) — 為之下, 'to act as their beneath'
the place below, the lower position
this (a demonstrative — not the verb 'to be')
to contend, to fight for place
potency — the power a thing has by being what it is

sentences.i: the best user of men puts himself beneath them. This is called the potency that does not contend; this is called the strength that lies in using men;
sentences.n:
為之下 is 'to act as their beneath' — 為 'act as', 之 'their', 下 'the lower place'. Wang Bi puts the reason bluntly: use men without putting yourself below them and their strength will not be used.

用人之力 can be cut two ways: 'the strength of men, used' — 用 [人之力] — or 'the strength that lies in using men', [用人] 之力. The parallel with 不爭之德 in the line before, 'the potency of not-contending', argues for the second, and that is what the English takes.

morph.gloss: to be matched with, to be paired to — the word for a consort, and for an ancestor sacrificed alongside a god
the utmost point, the far limit — properly the ridgepole at a roof's peak

sentences.l: this is called matching heaven — the utmost of old.
sentences.i: this is called being heaven's match, the furthest reach of antiquity.
sentences.n:
配 is the word for pairing: a consort matched to a ruler, and in the language of ritual an ancestor matched with Heaven and sacrificed to at its side. 配天 is therefore not 'to be like heaven' but to stand as heaven's counterpart.

古之極 is jammed on with nothing to join it — apposition, in the compressed manner of the whole chapter: 'this is called matching heaven; the utmost of old.' 極 is properly the ridgepole at the peak of a roof, hence the furthest point anything reaches.
